passage: Jahnavi, you asked why I stopped going to the prayer room, so here it is. I'm Akash. When Dada died in March, I was furious with God for letting it happen. Really angry. I'd lie awake asking, "Where were you?" I wrote it in a notebook so Mummy wouldn't hear. Part of me thought, if I'm this angry, I must still think someone is there to be angry at. Then I wasn't sure of anything. My friend Fayaz doesn't believe in God, and he told me he was furious at the universe when his aunt died. So it isn't only believers. I'm still angry, but I've stopped hiding it.

qa.q: What was Akash feeling toward God, and how did Akash express it?
qa.a: Akash felt angry and let down, asking "Where were you?" at night and writing it in a notebook. 🤍

qa.q: What could Akash do with the anger?
qa.a: Keep saying or writing it honestly, and share it with a friend like Jahnavi or a trusted adult instead of hiding it.

qa.q: How does Fayaz see anger after a loss?
qa.a: Fayaz was furious at the universe when his aunt died, so Fayaz sees it as something believers and non-believers both feel.

grounding: After a loss Akash is angry at God and speaks it aloud, learning that believers and non-believers both feel such anger.

passage:
"You're not coming to the prayer meeting?" Hemant stood in the doorway, dressed in white.

Gargi didn't look up from the bed. "No."

"It's for Dadu, Gargi."

"I know who it's for." Her voice cracked. "He prayed every single morning for sixty years. Every morning, bhaiya. And God let him get sick anyway, and let him go in three weeks. So what was the point?"

Hemant came and sat beside her. He didn't tell her to stop.

"I'm so angry," she said. "At God. Is that even allowed?"

"I think so. Dadu used to argue with God out loud when Dadi died. I heard him on the terrace."

Gargi looked up. "He did?"

"Yelling, almost. Then he kept praying. He said you can only be angry at someone you're talking to."

She cried then, properly. After a while she said, "Can I come and just sit at the back?"

"Of course."

qa.q: How long did Dadu pray every morning, according to Gargi?
qa.a: Gargi said he prayed every single morning for sixty years.

qa.q: What was Gargi feeling about Dadu's death?
qa.a: Gargi felt grief and deep anger at God for letting Dadu get sick and die after years of prayer.

qa.q: What did Hemant do that helped Gargi?
qa.a: Hemant sat with her, did not tell her to stop being angry, and shared how Dadu had argued with God too.

qa.q: What was it like for Hemant to hear his sister's anger?
qa.a: Hemant, also grieving, seems to understand it rather than being shocked, because he remembers Dadu's own anger on the terrace.

grounding: It shows a teen angry at God after a grandparent's death, learning that anger can be a way of speaking to God and can be said aloud.

passage:
When my dog Bruno died in Class 9, I stopped saying my prayers at night. I'm Varun. I know people lose parents and siblings, and a dog seems small next to that. But he'd slept at the foot of my bed for eleven years.

I remember lying awake thinking, if God is real, why would He let something so good die so slowly? I was angry in a way I'd never been. I felt guilty for being angry, too.

Zeenat, who sits next to me, noticed I was off. When I finally told her, I expected her to be shocked. She wasn't. She said, "After my Abbu's surgery went wrong, I was furious with Allah for months. I still prayed, but I shouted in my head."

It surprised me that someone who believes so much could be so angry.

So I started writing it down instead. Pages of it, just talking to God, or maybe to nobody. I still don't know which. But writing it helped more than staying silent.

qa.q: How long had Bruno slept at the foot of Varun's bed?
qa.a: Bruno had slept there for eleven years.

qa.q: What was Varun feeling after Bruno died?
qa.a: Varun felt grief and anger at God, and also guilty for feeling angry.

qa.q: What did Varun find helpful, and why?
qa.a: Writing the anger down in pages helped, because it gave the feeling somewhere to go instead of keeping it silent.

qa.q: How does Zeenat see anger at God?
qa.a: Zeenat sees it as something even believers feel, since she was furious with Allah after her Abbu's surgery but kept praying.

grounding: It shows a teen angry at God after a loss, finding that the anger can be written or spoken, and that believers feel it too.
